feed.title: Elena Verna on where product-led growth and enterprise sales collide
feed.summary: Verna's practitioner essay examines premature sales outreach, confusing signups with qualified demand and weakening self-serve adoption while chasing enterprise contracts.
feed.whyRelevant: Directly relevant to RevenueHero's lead handoffs and to products balancing self-serve adoption with enterprise sales. This is a practitioner's view, not a universal conversion benchmark.
feed.emailSubject: When should a product user actually hear from sales?
feed.emailBody:
Elena Verna's recent piece on PLG-to-enterprise friction is a useful discussion starter:
https://www.elenaverna.com/p/congrats-your-sales-problems-in-plg

Her argument is that a signup alone does not mean someone needs a sales conversation. Team adoption, usage expansion or governance needs can be more meaningful triggers.

What behavior most reliably tells you that a person would benefit from a human conversation at that point in their journey?
takeaways: Verna argues sales contact should respond to an account's emerging need, rather than follow every signup.
Moving existing self-serve revenue into an enterprise category can conceal added service costs without creating growth.
feed.discussionQuestion: What new customer value justifies human involvement, and how would you distinguish expansion from merely reclassifying revenue?

feed.title: Composio published the answers to the two questions every security review asks
feed.summary: Composio documents the two questions its enterprise security reviews always ask — whether staff can read customer tokens, and whether one customer can reach another’s data — and publishes the architectural answers rather than reassurance.
feed.whyRelevant: A portfolio company has published a reusable template for clearing enterprise security review. For any founder selling infrastructure into enterprises, this is a concrete artefact to copy rather than an opinion to consider.
feed.engagementMove: Forward as a template a peer already built, ask what their own two recurring questions are, and offer an introduction to the Composio team.
feed.emailSubject: A security-review template from inside the portfolio
feed.emailBody:
Composio published the two questions every enterprise security review asks them, and their answers:
https://composio.dev/blog/two-questions-every-security-review-asks-us

It is a useful template because it answers with architecture rather than reassurance. What are the two questions that keep coming back in your reviews? Happy to connect you with their team if useful.
takeaways: The two questions are named outright: “Can Composio staff read our users’ tokens?” and “Can another customer reach our data?”
The isolation unit is made explicit: “The project is the isolation boundary. Connected accounts, OAuth tokens, auth configs, and triggers each belong to exactly one project.”
Permissions are enforced in code, not prompts: “If you’ve said an agent may not delete, it cannot delete, regardless of what a prompt, a tool output, or the model’s own reasoning suggests.”
feed.discussionQuestion: What are the two questions your own security reviews always come back to, and is the answer written down anywhere a buyer can read it?

feed.title: What AI answers say about software pricing
feed.publisher: Profound · Kyle Poyar and Nikolas Laskaris
feed.summary: The authors tested 7,600 pricing responses across six AI engines and Cloud 100 companies, finding that company pricing pages often were not the primary cited source.
feed.whyRelevant: For RevenueHero, buyers may arrive at the demo with a preformed pricing view. For Spendflo, it is a prompt to examine how buyers research and compare vendors. Vendor-authored, time-bounded research.
feed.emailSubject: What buyers may believe before they request a demo
feed.emailBody:
This pricing study from Kyle Poyar and Profound is worth a look:
https://www.tryprofound.com/blog/what-ai-agents-really-think-about-your-pricing

They tested AI-generated pricing answers and found that official pricing pages often were not the main source. A practical experiment would be to audit a handful of common buyer questions against the actual offer.

Are pricing misunderstandings showing up earlier in your funnel, or only once a sales conversation begins?
takeaways: A visible pricing page may still hide its details from crawlers through rendering or interaction requirements.
The authors recommend consistent pricing, billing explanations and FAQs; their observed citation patterns are time-bounded.

feed.title: Together’s own write-up on why it backed Runable’s Series A
feed.summary: Shubham Gupta sets out why Together co-invested in Runable’s $21M Series A led by Susquehanna Venture Capital and Nexus, arguing that software creation is solved while the operational work that follows is not.
feed.whyRelevant: This is Together’s own published thesis, so sending it is a natural reason to write rather than a cold forward. It also gives SMB-facing founders in the portfolio a direct line to a peer working the same buyer.
feed.engagementMove: Send as “here is what we just published and why we think this way”, then offer to connect them with Umesh Kumar at Runable, who is working the same SMB buyer.
feed.emailSubject: What we published on Runable and the SMB gap
feed.emailBody:
We published our thinking behind Runable’s Series A:
https://www.together.fund/perspectives/insights/together-with-runable-helping-small-businesses-build-run-and-grow

The argument is that creating software has become cheap while everything after the first landing page has not moved. I would value your reaction, since you see this buyer far more closely than we do.
takeaways: The wedge is stated plainly: “nobody starts a business because they want a landing page.”
The gap Together is betting on: “everything after that first landing page has not moved.”
Scale cited for the round: “1.5 million users across the US, UK, Japan, and Brazil run their businesses on Runable,” and “Runable crossed $2M in ARR within three weeks of turning on monetization.”

feed.topic: Pricing · usage, seat, outcome and hybrid models
feed.summary: Bessemer profiles how Recall.ai (usage), Strella (seat), Graph AI (outcome) and Ada (hybrid) chose pricing models that held up through renewals, arguing durable pricing attaches to something the customer can check themselves.
feed.whyRelevant: Pricing is the decision most AI founders revisit under margin pressure, and this gives four named, dated examples rather than a framework. The verifiability test is a usable filter.
feed.engagementMove: Send with the verifiability test as the question, and offer a working session on pricing before their next renewal cycle.
feed.emailSubject: A pricing test: what can the customer verify themselves?
feed.emailBody:
Bessemer walked through how four AI companies landed on pricing that survived renewals:
https://www.bvp.com/atlas/durable-monetization-how-four-ai-founders-solved-the-pricing-puzzle

The useful filter is that durable pricing ties revenue to something a customer can independently verify rather than a claim. Which part of your value passes that test today?
takeaways: The organizing principle: “Durable AI pricing ties revenue to something a customer can independently verify, not to a claim.”
Usage pricing framed as alignment, from Recall.ai CEO David Gu: “if your product becomes very successful and you're now processing a lot of data, Recall.ai is going to cost more.”
Graph AI CEO Raghavendra Parvataraju describes the status quo it prices against: “customers are forced into a model where 75% of their spend goes toward human labor and only 25% toward the software.”
feed.discussionQuestion: What can your customer independently verify about the value you charge for, without taking your word for it?

feed.title: Segment choice at $10k MRR still predicts the business three years later
feed.topic: Company building · customer segment and retention
feed.summary: Using ChartMogul data on 1,043 SaaS and AI companies that reached $10k MRR by May 2023 and were still operating in May 2026, Poyar shows that the customer segment a company serves early tends to persist, and that segment shapes growth.
feed.whyRelevant: A dated, sourced answer to a decision most early founders make implicitly. It is most useful before a company has locked in its segment, which is exactly where several portfolio companies sit.
feed.engagementMove: Send to pre-scale founders with one question about which segment they are actually converting, not which one they target.
feed.emailSubject: The segment you pick early tends to stick
feed.emailBody:
Kyle Poyar looked at 1,043 companies from $10k MRR onward using ChartMogul data:
https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/startups-become-what-they-hunt

The finding that stayed with me is that 70% kept the same target customer three years later. Worth asking whether the segment converting today is the one you actually want.
takeaways: Segment choice is sticky: “When I mapped where companies started versus where they ended up, animal migrations turned out to be rare. 70% kept the same target customer.”
Mid-market compounds: “Companies that started as deer hunters and stayed there are growing revenue at an average of 22% year-over-year.”
Companies are grouped by average revenue per account: mouse under $30/month, rabbit $30–299, deer $300–2,999, elephant $3,000+.

feed.emailBody:
First Round’s guide to forward-deployed engineering is the most practical one I have read:
https://review.firstround.com/so-you-want-to-hire-a-forward-deployed-engineer/

Cut work that will not become product: if a use case is “endlessly iterating, and there was no clear path toward a software upside,” break the work off.

takeaways: Thirty percent of surveyed respondents reported waiting one to two weeks for authorization.
